title: One row on the langar floor
hookLine: caste, gender and race do not measure the soul
carry: the same light in every soul

lines: ONE STRIP OF CLOTH. ONE ROW.
THE SAME LADLE FOR EVERY PLATE.
cards: A long strip of cloth runs down the floor of a gurdwara hall. People sit on it in a row, shoulder to shoulder. A banker in a good coat.
A student with a backpack at her feet. A man who came in off the street because he was hungry. A grandmother who barely speaks the language of the room.

Someone walks down the line with a bucket of dal and fills every plate from the same ladle. Nobody's plate is first because of who they are. That row is the pangat, and it's a plain picture of today's idea.

teach.h: ASA: SEE THE LIGHT, NOT THE CASTE.
teach.b: First, the light. Early on this path you met Guru Nanak's line from Raag Asa; here it is again, in paraphrase: recognize the Lord's light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste.

The question a whole society used to sort people, what family were you born into, gets set aside. Not because birth is a secret, but because it measures the wrong thing. Second, a sharp question from a weaver.

teach.h: KABIR: WE ALL ARRIVE THE SAME WAY.
teach.b: The Granth keeps the verses of Kabir, a weaver by trade, and in one he turns to a man proud of high birth. In paraphrase: if you are so different, why didn't you come into the world some other way?
Everyone arrives the same way. The joke has a point. Third, one human family.

In the Akal Ustat, a work Sikhs keep in the Dasam Granth, a line Sikhs quote says, in paraphrase: recognize the whole human race as one. Caste, gender, color, nation: none of them is the scale a soul is weighed on.

teach.h: PANGAT: THE TEACHING ON THE FLOOR.
teach.b: Fourth, the floor. The Gurus didn't leave this a nice sentence. Sit in the row.
Eat from the same pot. Take the ladle and serve whoever is next. In the langar, equality stops being an idea and becomes dinner.
And equal souls isn't a claim that everyone is the same. The banker and the hungry man are still different people.
The light in each is the same light.

how: In the gurdwara's langar, Sikhs and guests sit together in rows called pangat and are served the same food, whatever their background; anyone may serve.

o: everyone is the same, with no differences at all
a seat of honor given to each guest in turn
the same light in everyone, whatever their birth

games.q: who said what about equal souls: tap the pairs.
p: see the light, don't ask the caste
we all arrive the same way
the row where everyone sits together

s: equal souls means everyone is the same
people stay different; the light in each is the same light.
the Granth keeps verses by Kabir, a weaver
and he asks a proud man why he didn't come into the world some other way.
in the langar row, the important guests are served first
the same ladle fills every plate down the row.

games.q: you're serving dal down the langar row. a well-known guest sits halfway along. what do you do?
o: skip ahead and serve the guest first.
serve the row in order, the same ladle for each plate.
give the guest a bigger portion.
games.why: in pangat nobody's plate is first because of who they are; the teaching is put on the floor.

practice: Bring to mind someone you tend to rank, a little above you or a little below: a boss, maybe, or someone who serves you lunch.

On the in-breath, see their face; on the out-breath, let the ranking drop, the way a coat slips off a chair. Then picture one ordinary way to treat them as an equal: their name used, their eyes met, their opinion asked.

wordCard.voice: Equal souls. Caste, gender and race don't measure the soul; the same light is in everyone, and the langar row puts it into practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pangat, the row in which everyone sits together to eat in the langar.

carryVoice: Your line: the same light in every soul. Not who are they, but where is the light in them. See you tomorrow.
